title: Ujiji, 1871: Two Diaries, One Voice
subtitle: Livingstone's last journeys, the Nyangwe massacre, the meeting with Stanley, and the carrying of his body to the coast, 1866–1874
intro: In 1866 David Livingstone went back to Africa to answer one question: where does the Nile begin? By 1871 he was 57 and ill, short of men and goods, and living beside a Zanzibari slaving caravan at Nyangwe, on a great river he hoped was the Nile and which was in fact the Congo. There he saw the traders' men fire into a crowded market on a July morning and kill hundreds of people, mostly women. He turned back to Ujiji, robbed and exhausted. There a New York Herald reporter who had been looking for him for most of a year walked into the town.

This chapter is built around one discovery about the record itself. Livingstone kept a raw field diary at Nyangwe, written in fading dye over a London newspaper. Later he rewrote it into a bound journal, and after his death his friend Horace Waller edited that journal into the Last Journals (1874). Between 2010 and 2012 the Livingstone Spectral Imaging Project and Livingstone Online (Adrian S. Wisnicki and colleagues) recovered the field diary. It differs from the published book: dates move, raids by his own men are toned down, his anger at the people he relied on is cut, and questions about his own followers at the massacre are dropped. Livingstone therefore appears here twice, as two eyes, so readers can set the first draft beside the public version.

The second puzzle is the meeting. Both men had lost count of days through fever. Livingstone's margin says 28 October 1871, Stanley's despatch says 3 November, his book says 10 November, and historians have argued for 27 and 29 October. Livingstone's field diary stops just before the meeting, and Stanley later tore the meeting pages out of his own diary. The greeting everyone knows appears only in Stanley's printed versions, and his biographer Tim Jeal thinks it was never spoken.

Most of the African voices come through European pages, and this chapter says so plainly. Dugumbe and Tagamoio, whose men fired at Nyangwe, are known only through Livingstone's accounts. Tippu Tip, who travelled with Livingstone in 1867, wrote a memoir decades later. Chuma and Susi, who decided to carry their master's body to the coast, left no writing of their own; their story reached print through Waller. Majwara, the boy alone with Livingstone when he died, was recorded by a consul. The exception is Jacob Wainwright, a freed Yao man from the Nasik mission school. He kept a diary of the death and the carrying, and its English pages were found and published only in 2019.

The record here is mixed. It includes diaries, a revised journal, a posthumous edition, consular letters, newspaper reports and a late memoir, and each eye's form says which is which. The last cluster is a second dating dispute: 1 May 1873, as Waller printed it, or the night of 4 May, as Wainwright and Majwara recorded. That matches the first: the people who were present and the people who edited the record often give different answers.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. In 1871, though, Livingstone's own dates were wrong. On 14 November 1871, using Stanley's almanac, he found he had run about three weeks ahead, and the 1871 Field Diary's new-moon entries confirm an error of about 20–21 days. Dates marked 'Livingstone's dating' (including 15 July for the massacre, the date historians use) are shown as he wrote them, and the true dates may be roughly three weeks earlier. The Livingstone–Stanley meeting has five candidate dates (27, 28 and 29 October; 3 and 10 November 1871). It is placed here at 3 November with 'range' precision. Livingstone's death is given as 1 May 1873 in the Last Journals and as the night of 4 May in Wainwright's diary and Majwara's testimony; both are shown.

eyes.name: David Livingstone (the 1871 Field Diary)
eyes.role: Scottish missionary-explorer, aged 57–58, ill, short of men, paper and ink, searching for the Nile's sources
eyes.side: British (independent; nominal consul, funded by the RGS, government and friends)
eyes.where: Nyangwe on the Lualaba (March–July 1871), then the road back to Ujiji
eyes.vantage_label: eyewitness of the massacre; the man Stanley came to find
eyes.form: diary (field diary, written in the moment)
eyes.authenticity: The raw diary, written across cut-up pages of The Standard (London, 24 November 1869) and scraps, first in iron-gall ink and then in a local dye he called 'Zingifure' that faded almost to nothing. It came home with his body in 1874, but stayed largely unread until the Livingstone Spectral Imaging Project imaged it in 2010 and Livingstone Online (ed. Adrian S. Wisnicki et al.) published it in 2011–12. Leaves are split between the David Livingstone Centre (Blantyre), the National Library of Scotland and the Bodleian. Because it was not published before 1929, it is digested here without quotation.
eyes.bio: This is Livingstone before he edited himself: hourly notes, anger at his own men and at the traders he depended on, and doubt. It is set apart from his later journal because the two versions of the same weeks differ, and the gap between them is the subject of this chapter.

eyes.name: David Livingstone (Unyanyembe Journal and Last Journals)
eyes.role: The same man, writing up his record for readers: first in the bound Unyanyembe Journal, then (after his death) as edited by Horace Waller
eyes.where: Ujiji and Unyanyembe (revision 1871–72), then Lake Bangweulu to Chitambo's (1872–73)
eyes.vantage_label: principal actor, revising his own eyewitness record
eyes.form: journal (fair copy revised from field diaries) and dated letters; published posthumously in edited form
eyes.authenticity: The Unyanyembe Journal (c. 800 pages, 28 January 1866 – 5 March 1872) is a 'second stage' record that trims, re-dates and reworks the field diaries; some pages are in Stanley's hand, and Stanley carried it to England in 1872. The Last Journals (John Murray, 1874), edited by Horace Waller, are built on it and on the later notebooks, with Waller's linking narrative. Where field diary and journal disagree, both are shown here.
eyes.bio: The Livingstone the Victorian public knew: measured, pious, outraged at the slave trade. He is given his own column so readers can see one voice in two forms, and watch dates move, a raid get softer, and the question of his own men's conduct fade.

eyes.name: Henry Morton Stanley
eyes.role: Welsh-born (as John Rowlands) American newspaper correspondent, aged about 30, leading a New York Herald caravan
eyes.where: Bagamoyo to Unyanyembe to Ujiji; on Lake Tanganyika with Livingstone; back to the coast
eyes.vantage_label: the finder; principal actor and publicist
eyes.form: diary, newspaper despatches, and a book (memoir written later)
eyes.authenticity: Stanley's field diaries are in the H. M. Stanley Archives (King Baudouin Foundation, on deposit at the Royal Museum for Central Africa, Tervuren), many published in Leduc-Grimaldi and Newman, Finding Dr. Livingstone (2020). The pages covering the meeting were torn out, and nothing in Livingstone's letters mentions the famous greeting. How I Found Livingstone (1872) was written up for publication and gives dates and scenes that his despatches and diary do not support exactly. Treat the book as a rewritten account.
eyes.bio: A workhouse boy from Denbigh who reinvented himself in America, fought on both sides of the US Civil War and deserted twice, and became a star reporter. Stanley needed the meeting to be a scoop. His record is vivid, self-serving and, at the key moment, missing.

sources.title: How I Found Livingstone (1872), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Dugumbe (Hassani) and the traders at Nyangwe
eyes.role: Leader of a large Zanzibari-Swahili ivory and slaving caravan camped at Nyangwe; Tagamoio was his principal under-trader
eyes.where: His camp beside the Nyangwe market, right bank of the Lualaba
eyes.vantage_label: the traders whose men fired; known only through Livingstone
eyes.form: reported speech and acts in Livingstone's diary, journal and letters (no record of his own)
eyes.authenticity: No writing by Dugumbe or Tagamoio is known. Everything here comes through Livingstone, whose three massacre accounts treat Dugumbe differently: the letter to Granville credits him with stopping the shooting and saving 21 people, while the field diary, the editors note, does not clearly clear him. This column is flagged as a voice heard only through the traveller.
eyes.bio: Dugumbe gave Livingstone food, goods and help with canoes, and his people were the ones who fired on the market. Keeping him as a separate eye, even second-hand, shows how much Livingstone's view of 'the Arabs' depended on which one he was talking to and which version he was writing.

sources.title: The Third Massacre Narrative (Livingstone Online)
Livingstone in 1871 (Livingstone Online)

eyes.name: Tippu Tip (Hamed bin Muhammed el-Murjebi)
eyes.role: Zanzibari-Swahili trader in ivory and enslaved people, of Omani descent, then building an empire west of Lake Tanganyika
eyes.where: Itawa / Lake Mweru region (1867); later Kasongo and Nyangwe (Manyema)
eyes.vantage_label: the trade network around Livingstone, remembered decades later
eyes.authenticity: His autobiography (Maisha ya Hamed bin Muhammed) was written in Zanzibar after he retired. It was transcribed into Roman script and translated into German by Heinrich Brode, who published it in 1902–03, with an English version of Brode's book in 1907; W. H. Whiteley later made a Swahili–English edition, and François Bontinck produced an annotated French edition (1974). It is a retrospective account shaped for its readers, and its chronology of the 1860s is not reliable to the day.
eyes.bio: He travelled with Livingstone through Itawa in 1867 and helped him on his way. In 1876 he escorted Stanley down the Lualaba from Nyangwe, the same river and town. His memoir is the closest thing to a self-account from the trade Livingstone condemned, and it was written for European readers late in the colonial period.

sources.title: Tippoo Tib: the story of his career in Central Africa (Brode, Eng. tr. 1907)
Review of Bontinck's annotated L'Autobiographie de Hamed ben Mohammed el-Murjebi Tippo Tip (1974)
The 'Autobiography' of Tippu Tip: Geography, Genre and the African Indian Ocean

eyes.name: John Kirk
eyes.role: Physician and botanist from Livingstone's Zambezi expedition; acting, then full, British consul and political agent at Zanzibar
eyes.where: Zanzibar and the mainland coast at Bagamoyo
eyes.vantage_label: the coast: supplier, consul, later the target of blame
eyes.form: dated letters (official and to the RGS)
eyes.authenticity: His consular despatches and letters to the RGS are contemporary and dated; two were printed in the Proceedings of the RGS for 8 May 1871. His side of the quarrel with Stanley survives in consular papers and his later letters.
eyes.bio: Kirk was Livingstone's old colleague and his supply line, and the Banian men who caused Livingstone such trouble at Nyangwe had been hired through him. Stanley decided Kirk had neglected his old chief and said so, and Livingstone turned against him. In 1873 Kirk secured the Sultan's treaty closing the Zanzibar slave market.

sources.title: Proceedings of the RGS, 8 May 1871: letters from Dr. Kirk
Livingstone's letter to Waller, 5 Feb 1871, annotations (on Kirk)

eyes.name: James Gordon Bennett Jr and the New York Herald
eyes.role: Proprietor of the New York Herald, who paid for Stanley's search; the paper that printed it
eyes.where: New York and Paris; the Herald's London office
eyes.vantage_label: the press abroad: buyer and seller of the story
eyes.authenticity: Bennett left no diary of the affair. The famous commission scene ('Find Livingstone', Paris, 1869) comes from Stanley's own later telling. The Herald's printed reports are dated and real, but they were edited for sales and print Stanley's polished version of events.
eyes.bio: The Herald turned an elderly missionary who had not been heard from for years into a transatlantic news event, using the 1866 Atlantic cable. It is included as the eye that turned the encounter into a headline, and the version of the greeting most people remember comes from its page.

sources.title: Rubery, On Henry Morton Stanley's Search for Dr. Livingstone (BRANCH)
Nature, 2 April 1874: The Death of Dr. Livingstone (Herald telegram)

eyes.name: Jacob Wainwright
eyes.role: Yao man, born Yamuza, enslaved as a youth, freed by a British naval patrol and schooled at the Church Missionary Society school at Nasik, India; recruited for Livingstone's last party
eyes.where: With Livingstone to Chitambo's; with the body to the coast and on to England
eyes.vantage_label: at the deathbed camp; diarist of the carrying
eyes.language: English (his full diary known since 1874 in German translation)
eyes.authenticity: His diary of the journey was known from a German translation published in 1874; the original was thought lost until manuscript pages in English, partly in his hand, held at the David Livingstone Birthplace (Blantyre), were digitised and published by Livingstone Online / One More Voice in 2019–20. A further version was edited for the Hakluyt Society (2007). The loose diary pages are catalogued with other hands (James Christie, A. Paterson), so authorship of every page is not certain.
eyes.bio: The only African member of the party to write a diary in the moment, and the only African pall-bearer at the Abbey. His pages show the grief and the hard decisions, and also the mission-school prejudices of his education. Later he taught, worked as a porter in Zanzibar, and served the LMS at Urambo, where he died in 1892.

sources.title: Extract from Diary (One More Voice, liv_000074)
Extract from Diary (One More Voice, liv_000075)

Rare Diary of Livingstone's Death (Blantyre Project)

eyes.name: James Chuma and Abdullah Susi
eyes.role: Livingstone's two longest-serving followers: Chuma, a Yao boy freed in 1861; Susi, from Shupanga on the Zambezi, a woodcutter on the Zambezi expedition, later baptised David (1886)
eyes.where: With Livingstone from 1866; leaders of the party that carried his body to the coast
eyes.vantage_label: closest companions; leaders of the carrying
eyes.form: oral testimony recorded by others (Waller's narrative in the Last Journals, consular letters)
eyes.language: Swahili and other East African languages, recorded in English
eyes.authenticity: Neither left a diary. Their account of the last days and the march is known mainly from Horace Waller's narrative chapters in the Last Journals (1874), put together from interviews during their stay in England in 1874, and from consular summaries in Zanzibar. It comes through a European editor and is flagged accordingly.
eyes.bio: Without them there would be no Westminster grave, no surviving notebooks and no Last Journals. They decided to carry the body and papers more than 1,000 miles to the coast against advice. They were paid off at the coast and only belatedly honoured, receiving RGS medals in June 1874.

sources.title: The Last Journals, vol. II (narrative of the last days)
RGS fact sheet: James Chuma
RGS fact sheet: Abdullah Susi

eyes.name: Majwara (via Frederick Holmwood)
eyes.role: A boy given to Livingstone by Stanley, who served as his personal attendant; the only person in the hut when he died
eyes.where: Inside Livingstone's hut near Chitambo's village, Ilala
eyes.form: oral testimony in a dated consular letter (Holmwood to Frere, 12 March 1874)
eyes.authenticity: Recorded by Frederick Holmwood at the Zanzibar consulate, possibly through an interpreter, and checked against Susi and the Nasik men; printed in the Proceedings of the RGS on 13 April 1874; edited by One More Voice (2021). Holmwood himself calls the narrative very unconnected.
eyes.bio: Majwara's testimony, taken down within a year, offers the most intimate view of the last days and supports the 4 May date for the death. It survives because a consul thought it worth sending to Sir Bartle Frere, so like most African voices here it reached print through a European official.

sources.title: Majwara's Account of the Last Journey and Death of Dr. Livingstone (One More Voice)

eyes.name: Horace Waller
eyes.role: Former lay superintendent of the Universities' Mission on the Zambezi, Anglican clergyman, anti-slavery campaigner, Livingstone's friend and posthumous editor
eyes.where: England: London and Newstead Abbey (Nottinghamshire), working with Chuma and Susi
eyes.vantage_label: the editor at home, shaping the record
eyes.form: edited text (posthumous edition with editorial narrative)
eyes.authenticity: Waller's Last Journals (dated 1874, on sale by January 1875) combine the Unyanyembe Journal, the later notebooks and his own linking narrative from interviews with Chuma and Susi. He condensed and smoothed the text throughout. The book is real but edited, not a raw diary, and is flagged as an edition.
eyes.bio: Waller sent Livingstone newspapers and letters that reached him at Bambarre in February 1871, and received letters back. After 1874 he decided what the world would read of the last journey. His editing produced the familiar picture of Livingstone as a martyr, and the spectral-imaging work of the 2010s has been reading behind it.

sources.title: The Last Journals of David Livingstone (Project Gutenberg)
Livingstone's letter to Horace Waller, Bambarre, 5 Feb 1871 (Livingstone Online)

entries.headline: The last journal opens at Zanzibar
entries.digest: The Unyanyembe Journal, and with it the Last Journals, begins at Zanzibar as Livingstone prepares his final expedition: up the Rovuma and inland to settle where the Nile begins. He has sepoys, men from Johanna, freed boys from the Nasik school, and baggage animals. Within months most of the animals are dead and many of the men have deserted.
entries.source_note: Unyanyembe Journal date range (28 Jan 1866 – 5 Mar 1872), Livingstone Online node/200; Last Journals vol. I opens Zanzibar 28 Jan 1866.

entries.headline: The trader who would rule Manyema meets the missionary
entries.digest: Tippu Tip's memoir, written decades later in Zanzibar, recalls meeting the Englishman in the Itawa country, where caravans were fighting over ivory with the chief Nsama. He presents himself as Livingstone's protector, and Livingstone did travel for a while under the shelter of the Zanzibari caravans he despised. The memoir's dates for this period are not exact.
entries.source_note: Tippu Tip autobiography (Brode, 1902–03; Eng. tr. 1907); dating per Bontinck's annotated edition. Exact day not established.

entries.headline: 'Find Livingstone': the commission, as Stanley told it
entries.digest: In Stanley's later telling, Bennett summoned him to Paris and told him to find Livingstone, whatever it cost, after first covering the Suez Canal opening and touring the Near East. Bennett left no account of his own. The story of the order became part of the legend Stanley's book sold.
entries.source_note: Rubery (BRANCH) quoting the instruction to 'Find out Livingstone'; How I Found Livingstone, introduction. Scene known only from Stanley.

entries.headline: Letters from Waller reach Bambarre, and Livingstone writes back
entries.digest: Lame with foot ulcers, stuck at Bambarre since July 1870, Livingstone has just received newspapers and letters from Horace Waller, his first news from home in a long time. He writes back at length. The letter will eventually travel to England in Stanley's baggage and reach Waller, who will later edit Livingstone's journals.
entries.source_note: Letter to Horace Waller, Bambarre, 5 Feb 1871 (Livingstone Online node/231); receipt of Waller's packet 4 Feb 1871 per 'Livingstone in 1871' (node/233).

entries.place: Zanzibar, after a visit to Bagamoyo
entries.headline: Kirk finds Livingstone's relief caravan stuck on the coast
entries.digest: Kirk reports that the stores sent for Livingstone were still sitting at Bagamoyo, short of porters, after cholera had killed many people in Unyamwezi. He crossed to the mainland himself to get the loads moving. No caravan coming down from Unyanyembe had any news of Livingstone beyond the fact that he had gone west.
entries.source_note: Kirk to RGS, 18 Feb 1871, printed Proc. RGS 8 May 1871 (galton.org PDF).

entries.headline: Kirk forwards word from Ujiji
entries.digest: A second letter forwards news that has reached Ujiji: Livingstone is believed to be in Manyema, waiting for men and supplies Kirk sent the year before. Those supplies are said to have reached Ujiji and to be going on to him. Kirk adds that he has not had time to check the place-names with Arab travellers before the mail closes.
entries.source_note: Kirk to RGS, 10 Mar 1871, Proc. RGS 8 May 1871.

entries.headline: Stanley's caravan marches inland
entries.digest: After weeks in Zanzibar buying cloth, beads and wire and hiring men (and meeting Consul Kirk), Stanley leads his Herald expedition out of Bagamoyo toward Unyanyembe. It is one of the largest caravans of the season, and he keeps its real purpose quiet. Fever, desertions and a local war will slow him for months.
entries.source_note: Date as commonly given (History.com 'Stanley begins search for Livingstone', 21 March); How I Found Livingstone. Not checked against the Tervuren diary.

entries.headline: Arrival at the great market on the Lualaba
entries.digest: Livingstone reaches Nyangwe, where a huge river flows north. He thinks it may be the Nile, though it was in fact the upper Congo. He needs canoes to follow it. The diary describes the market, where thousands of people gather every fourth day, and the Bagenya (Wagenya) people of the river, who distrust a stranger who arrived with the slave-traders' caravans.
entries.source_note: Livingstone Online, 'Livingstone in 1871' and 'The Manuscript of the 1871 Field Diary' (stay at Nyangwe 30 Mar – 20 Jul 1871).

entries.date_display: 30 April 1871 (field diary) — moved to 25 April in the Unyanyembe Journal
entries.headline: His own men are the danger
entries.digest: The field diary records, angrily, the violent and murderous behaviour of the Banian-hired men sent up from the coast. They threaten mutiny, refuse rations and talk of killing. When Livingstone copied this into his bound journal he moved the passage to 25 April and toned it down, the first of several small shifts in the record of these weeks.
entries.source_note: 'Livingstone in 1871' (node/233): diary dated 30 April, moved to 25 April in UJ; R&D World report on sanitised passages.

entries.headline: Cheated over a canoe, Livingstone sends men to force restitution
entries.digest: A deal for a canoe with a local man, Kalenga, falls through and Livingstone feels swindled. In his fury he sends his men to make Kalenga pay, and Kalenga runs away. The field diary shows a Livingstone using force to get what he needed, a side the later versions do not dwell on.
entries.source_note: 'Livingstone in 1871' (node/233).

entries.headline: Dugumbe offers to help find a canoe
entries.digest: In Livingstone's June and July entries, the newly arrived trader Dugumbe offers to help him buy a canoe and to supply him with goods. He also talks with Livingstone's men about going on, which Livingstone half hopes and half fears. As always, the conversation comes to us only in Livingstone's words.
entries.source_note: Livingstone Online, Three Versions page (field diary June–July entries on Dugumbe).

entries.headline: His men refuse to go beyond the Lomame
entries.digest: His followers refuse to go any further west, toward the Lomame river. Without them, and without a canoe, Livingstone cannot follow the Lualaba. Meanwhile, the diary notes, Dugumbe's man Manilla has been raiding villages across the river on behalf of the Bagenya chief Kimburu, and the area is close to violence.
entries.source_note: Livingstone Online, Three Versions page and 'Livingstone in 1871'.

entries.headline: Firing into the market crowd
entries.digest: On a hot market morning, armed men from the traders' camp open fire on the crowd of mostly women gathered to trade. People run into the river and drown trying to reach canoes. Livingstone records what he sees as it happens and later counts seventeen villages burning across the river. The traders themselves estimated 400 to 500 dead. The entries become almost hourly from this point.
entries.source_note: Livingstone Online 1871 Field Diary edition (node/163) and 'Livingstone in 1871' (node/233).

entries.date_display: 15 July 1871 (as Livingstone told it to Granville in November)
entries.headline: Dugumbe calls off the shooting, as Livingstone reports
entries.digest: In Livingstone's official account, Dugumbe's chief under-trader Tagamoio and his men did the shooting, and Dugumbe ordered his people to stop, sending a canoe that pulled 21 people from the water. Dugumbe also warned Livingstone not to start a blood feud by taking revenge. The field diary does not clearly clear Dugumbe. Tagamoio was never punished and kept his power at Nyangwe into the 1890s.
entries.source_note: 'The Third Massacre Narrative' (letter to Granville, 14 Nov 1871), node/150; editors' note in node/233.

entries.headline: The day after: horror, and the name Tagamoio
entries.digest: Burning and killing continue into the next day, with more villages alight. Livingstone writes of the horror of it and names Tagamoio for the first time. He also wonders, in the diary only, about the part his own men played. In the published versions he states firmly that they took no part.
entries.source_note: 'Livingstone in 1871' (node/233); R&D World (Wisnicki: evidence 'hints' at his men's involvement; Jeal unconvinced).

entries.headline: He turns back toward Ujiji
entries.digest: Having decided on the 17th that he cannot go on in the company of men who did this, Livingstone leaves Nyangwe for Ujiji, more than 200 miles east, without seeing the Lualaba's course. The march is miserable. He is often ill and in danger, and suspected of being a slaver himself because he is travelling with the traders.
entries.source_note: 'Livingstone in 1871' (decision 17 July, departure 20 July); node/163.

entries.date_display: 23 October 1871 (Livingstone's dating; probably about three weeks early by the true calendar)
entries.headline: Back at Ujiji, and robbed
entries.digest: Livingstone reaches Ujiji worn out. The goods sent up for him have been sold off by the man left in charge of them, so he has almost nothing to trade for food. In the journal, written up for readers, this is the low point before a rescue, and the narrative is shaped toward the arrival that follows.
entries.source_note: Field diary records 23 Oct as arrival (date essay, node/204); manuscript 1871m covers 23 Oct – 3 Nov (node/189).

entries.date_display: late October 1871 (field diary fragment 1871m, Livingstone's dating)
entries.headline: The last field-diary scrap: someone is coming
entries.digest: The last fragment of the 1871 field diary, now in the Bodleian, records news of a white man's caravan approaching Ujiji. Its final dated entry, '3 November' by Livingstone's count, corresponds by the editors' working to mid-October. The diary ends here, just before the meeting it is famous for.
entries.source_note: Manuscript of the 1871 Field Diary (node/189): leaf 1871m:[1], 'the Stanley approach entry'; date essay (node/204).

entries.date_display: '28 October' written in the margin (Unyanyembe Journal)
entries.headline: The meeting, as Livingstone wrote it up
entries.digest: In a long journal entry headed 24 October, Livingstone describes the arrival of the American caravan 'one morning' and his surprise and gratitude. The date '28 October' appears in the margin of the next page. He does not mention the greeting that became famous. His account is warm, and the dating is vague.
entries.source_note: Date essay (node/204): UJ entry dated 24 Oct with '28 October' in margin; Bridges on the ambiguity of 'one morning'.

entries.headline: The despatch puts the meeting on 3 November
entries.digest: Stanley's despatch to the Herald, dated 10 November, says he met Livingstone a week earlier, on 3 November. Historians disagree about whether that figure is a raw date or one he had already corrected. Both men had lost count of days through fever. Jeal argues the despatch was in fact written after mid-November.
entries.source_note: Date essay (node/204), Bontinck (1979) and Jeal readings.

entries.headline: The book's date, and the most famous line in exploration
entries.digest: In How I Found Livingstone, Stanley sets the meeting on 10 November. He describes doffing his hat to a pale, grey-bearded man in a faded consular cap and greeting him with the line that made both men famous. The diary pages for these days were torn out, Livingstone never mentions the phrase, and Tim Jeal concludes it was probably invented later.
entries.source_note: How I Found Livingstone (1872); date essay node/204; Jeal via NYRB 2007 and Rubery (BRANCH). Day itself disputed.

entries.headline: Three weeks lost, and the massacre told to the Foreign Secretary
entries.digest: Using Stanley's almanac, Livingstone realises his dates have been about three weeks ahead. The same day he writes his long letter to Earl Granville describing the Nyangwe killings. It is the only account of the massacre published in his lifetime, appearing in the 1872 Parliamentary Papers, and it helped push Britain to press Zanzibar on the slave trade.
entries.source_note: Date essay (node/204: Ramadan, 14 Nov 1871, 21 days ahead); 'The Third Massacre Narrative' (node/150).

entries.headline: A new notebook opens, with company
entries.digest: Field Diary XIV, a small Letts notebook written mostly in pencil, opens at Ujiji. Livingstone's first mention of his visitor is a note about Stanley's fever. The entries are short now, mostly weather, dates and geography, because he has a companion and post from Europe and America again.
entries.source_note: Field Diary XIV: An Overview (node/195), date range 14 Nov 1871 – 14 Sep 1872.

entries.headline: Twenty-eight days on the lake: the Rusizi flows in
entries.digest: Stanley and Livingstone take a canoe to the north end of the lake to check whether the Rusizi carries Tanganyika's water north toward the Nile. They find it flows into the lake, so the lake is not the Nile's source by that route. In his book, Stanley says the old man still clings to his Nile theory about the Lualaba. They are back at Ujiji on 12 December, by Stanley's count.
entries.source_note: How I Found Livingstone ch. XIII (28-day cruise; return 'on the 12th'); Field Diary XIV overview (Rusizi flows into lake).

entries.headline: The Rusizi settles one question and leaves the big one open
entries.digest: Livingstone's notebook records the trip north and the Rusizi's inflow, ruling out Tanganyika's north end as a direct feeder of the Nile. For him, the true answer still lies on the Lualaba and in the fountains he believed lay south-west. Both men were wrong about that river, which would turn out to be the Congo.
entries.source_note: Field Diary XIV overview (node/195).

entries.headline: Parting at Unyanyembe
entries.digest: After reaching Unyanyembe on 18 February, where stores were waiting, Stanley leaves for the coast. He refuses to wait longer, and Livingstone refuses to go home. Stanley carries letters and the bound Unyanyembe Journal for Livingstone's family. In his book the farewell becomes a scene of near-filial grief.
entries.source_note: Field Diary XIV overview (node/195: Unyanyembe 18 Feb, Stanley leaves 14 Mar 1872); UJ note of dispatch dated 14 Mar 1872 (node/200).

entries.headline: The journal goes home without him
entries.digest: Livingstone notes that he is sending his journal to England with Stanley. The volume, with some pages in Stanley's hand, is the revised record that will become the backbone of the Last Journals. The raw Nyangwe diary stays in his tin case and goes on with him.
entries.source_note: Unyanyembe Journal overview (node/200).

entries.headline: Blamed by the man he outranked
entries.digest: Back on the coast, Stanley lets it be known, and later prints, that Kirk had let Livingstone's supplies and men sit idle and handled them badly. Livingstone, reading Stanley's letters and remembering the Banian men Kirk had hired, turns against his old friend. The Livingstone Online editors judge that Stanley came to believe this wrongly.
entries.source_note: Annotations to Livingstone's letter to Waller, 5 Feb 1871 (node/231). Exact dates of the Zanzibar confrontation not verified.

entries.headline: 'Livingstone Safe': the scoop fills a page
entries.digest: The New York Herald prints Stanley's story, filling its whole third page, with the greeting and Livingstone's reply. Thanks to the Atlantic cable it is told almost at once in Britain too, where the press is part admiring and part resentful that an American got there first. Some papers, the Standard among them, suggest the Livingstone letters may be forged.
entries.source_note: Rubery, BRANCH (Herald 2 July 1872, whole third page; Standard first to allege forgery).

entries.headline: The Nasik men arrive
entries.digest: Jacob Wainwright arrives at Unyanyembe with the men Stanley hired and sent up from the coast for Livingstone's last push south-west. By the end of August the party has left for the country south of Lake Tanganyika and toward Lake Bangweulu.
entries.source_note: Majwara's account (departure c. end Aug 1872); Wainwright biography (recruited via Stanley). Arrival day not verified.

entries.headline: The last entry
entries.digest: The last entry in the notebook is a few broken words. He is exhausted and has sent men to buy milk goats, and the party is camped by a river in the swamps south of Bangweulu. He can no longer walk or ride and is being carried. These words, printed by Waller, closed the Last Journals' diary text.
entries.source_note: Last Journals vol. II, final entry 27 Apr 1873; Majwara's account (carried on a kitanda).

entries.headline: Found kneeling by the bed, before dawn
entries.digest: In Waller's narrative from Susi and Chuma, the boy on watch calls them in the small hours. They find Livingstone kneeling by his bed, his head in his hands, dead. The date in the Last Journals and on most memorials is 1 May. They gather the men, take charge of the papers and instruments, and decide to keep the body.
entries.source_note: Last Journals vol. II narrative; Blantyre Project summary. Date disputed (see 4 May entries).

entries.headline: Only the boy was there
entries.digest: Majwara tells the consul that in his last days Livingstone was in great pain, could keep nothing down and could barely see. He had been carried back from a village that refused them shelter to a hut built for him. Majwara was alone with him on the night he died and could not say when he stopped breathing. The party first reckoned the date as 28 April and corrected it to 4 May when they compared diaries at Unyanyembe.
entries.source_note: Holmwood to Frere, 12 Mar 1874, Proc. RGS 13 Apr 1874 (One More Voice liv_020053).

entries.headline: Salt, sun and a carved tree
entries.digest: Wainwright's diary dates the death to the night of 4 May. Next day the men take out the organs and salt the body, noting the state of the lungs and the dark blood, and bury the inner organs with a Christian service under a tree. They carve the tree with Livingstone's name, the date and the names of their leaders. A two-day mourning in local style follows.
entries.source_note: One More Voice liv_000074 (4 May death; 5 May salting; tree inscription); Smithsonian/Guardian 2019 report.

entries.headline: The slave market is closed
entries.digest: Under heavy British pressure applied through Kirk, Sultan Barghash signs a treaty ending the seaborne slave trade and closing Zanzibar's public slave market. Livingstone's Nyangwe letter, printed in 1872, had helped build the public pressure. Livingstone, in the swamps of Bangweulu, never learned of it.
entries.source_note: Treaty of 1873 (R&D World: the consul pressured the sultan in 1873); date 5 June 1873 as usually given, not checked against the treaty text here.

entries.headline: Crossing the Luapula with the dead
entries.digest: The diary records reaching the Luapula with many men sick. On the far bank, lions attack the camp at night and kill a donkey. The party carrying the dried, bark-wrapped body moves slowly, crossing flooded country and avoiding villages that might not let a corpse pass.
entries.source_note: One More Voice liv_000074, entry 25 June 1873.

entries.headline: They refuse to bury him
entries.digest: At Unyanyembe they meet the RGS relief expedition under Lieutenant Verney Lovett Cameron, who tells them to bury the body there. They refuse, and keep going toward the coast with the body and most of the papers. Here, comparing records, they also correct the date of death.
entries.source_note: Smithsonian 2019 (Cameron tried to make them bury the body; they refused); Majwara's account (dates compared at Unyanyembe). Day not verified.

entries.headline: At the coast after about nine months
entries.digest: The party reaches Bagamoyo and hands the body to British officials, ending a march of roughly 1,000 miles that cost several lives. Chuma and Susi are paid off and dismissed. The body and papers go to Zanzibar and then to England, with Jacob Wainwright alone of the carriers going with them.
entries.source_note: Smithsonian 2019; Blantyre Project ('brusquely dismissed'); exact day not verified.

entries.headline: The consul writes down the boy's story
entries.digest: Frederick Holmwood, standing in for the ailing consul-general, sends Sir Bartle Frere a summary of Majwara's account, checked with Susi and the Nasik men. He estimates the place of death at about 11.25 degrees south and 27 east, subject to correction. He notes that Arthur Laing has charge of the remains and the diaries on the voyage.
entries.source_note: One More Voice liv_020053.

entries.date_display: Sunday 29 March 1874 (Suez telegram; printed in Nature 2 April)
entries.headline: The Herald scoops the death too
entries.digest: A telegram from Suez, obtained through the New York Herald's London office, gives British papers the first details of Livingstone's death as the body travels up the Red Sea. Nature reprints the news. The paper that had 'found' Livingstone now reports how he died.
entries.source_note: Nature 9, 424 (2 April 1874), 'The Death of Dr. Livingstone'.

entries.headline: The only African pall-bearer
entries.digest: Wainwright, who travelled with the coffin from Zanzibar, is one of eight pall-bearers at the Abbey funeral, and the only African among them. The brass on the grave will credit 'faithful hands', but Chuma and Susi are not there. They arrive in England only later that year.
entries.quote: Brought by faithful hands over land and sea
entries.source_note: Westminster Abbey commemoration page (burial 18 April 1874; inscription); Jacob Wainwright biography (pall-bearer).

entries.headline: The finder carries the coffin
entries.digest: Stanley, now famous and still distrusted in parts of the British establishment, is among the pall-bearers. Within months he is preparing a new expedition, partly backed by the Herald, to settle the Nile and Lualaba questions that Livingstone had left open.
entries.source_note: Blantyre Project (Stanley among the pall-bearers); Westminster Abbey page (date).

entries.headline: Editing the dead man's journals with the men who carried him
entries.digest: Chuma and Susi are brought to England by James Young and stay at William Webb's Newstead Abbey, where Waller questions them for the narrative of the final months. In June they receive RGS medals. Waller writes their memories into the Last Journals as his own linking prose, the main surviving record of what they saw.
entries.source_note: Chuma and Susi biographies (Newstead Abbey; returned Oct 1874); RGS fact sheet (medals June 1874).

entries.headline: The Last Journals appear
entries.digest: Waller's two volumes are published, combining the bound journal, the later notebooks and the carriers' narrative into a single martyr's story. The raw Nyangwe pages, written in faded dye over a London newspaper, stay among the family papers. More than a century later spectral imaging shows how different the first draft was.
entries.source_note: Livingstone Online 'Aftermath' (Murray estimate book, Quarterly Review advert Jan 1875).

entries.headline: The trader's own story reaches print
entries.digest: Retired in Zanzibar, Tippu Tip's Swahili memoir is published by Heinrich Brode in Roman script with a German translation, and an English version of Brode's book follows in 1907. It covers his ivory empire in Manyema, his dealings with Livingstone and Stanley, and his governorship at Stanley Falls. It was written after the Congo Free State had destroyed the Zanzibari trading order, and with that in mind.
entries.source_note: Tippu Tip biography; Brode, Tippoo Tib (Eng. 1907). Composition date debated (c. 1890s–1900s).

convergences.label: The Nyangwe market massacre
convergences.note: The same morning in three registers: the field diary written as it happened, with doubts about his own men; the official letter that makes Tagamoio the villain and Dugumbe the rescuer; and the polished journal. The traders' and victims' own accounts do not survive in writing.

convergences.label: The meeting at Ujiji — five candidate dates
convergences.note: Livingstone's margin says 28 October; Stanley's despatch says 3 November; his book says 10 November; scholars have argued for 27 and 29 October. Livingstone's field diary stops just before the meeting, and Stanley's diary pages for it are missing.

convergences.label: Ujiji: the calendar corrected, the massacre reported
convergences.note: On one day Livingstone learns he is three weeks out, writes the Granville letter, and starts a fresh notebook. The revised record begins where the raw one ends.

convergences.label: Together on Lake Tanganyika
convergences.note: The two men share one canoe and reach the same finding about the Rusizi. Stanley writes it up as adventure and Livingstone as geography, and both keep wrong theories about the Lualaba.

convergences.label: The death at Chitambo's — 1 May or 4 May?
convergences.note: Waller's narrative from Susi and Chuma gives 1 May. Wainwright's diary and Majwara's testimony give the night of 4 May, after an earlier reckoning of 28 April. The tree inscription carried 4 May. Like the Ujiji date, the date of death depends on whose record you follow.

convergences.label: The body reaches the coast
convergences.note: The carriers' achievement and their dismissal happen in the same week. Only Wainwright, the one who wrote English, goes on to London.

convergences.label: Westminster Abbey
convergences.note: Finder, carrier, press and editor all meet at the grave. The inscription thanks faithful hands without naming them.

ties.note: The same author at two stages: raw field notes and the revised record he meant readers to see. Dates, emphasis and his men's role shift between them.
Four months together at Ujiji, on the lake and at Unyanyembe; Stanley wrote pages in Livingstone's journal and carried it home.
Stanley blamed Kirk for neglecting Livingstone's supplies, and the quarrel turned Livingstone against his old Zambezi colleague.
Bennett paid for the search, and the Herald printed and shaped Stanley's version, including the greeting.
Livingstone lived beside Dugumbe's camp at Nyangwe and depended on his help, and was there when his men fired on the market.
They travelled together in Itawa in 1867; Tippu Tip later escorted Stanley from Nyangwe in 1876.
Both belonged to the Zanzibari trading network that made Nyangwe and Kasongo its base in Manyema.
They carried the body together. Wainwright's diary and Chuma and Susi's testimony to Waller give different dates for the death.
Majwara's testimony confirmed the 4 May date that Wainwright reached by comparing diaries at Unyanyembe.
At Newstead Abbey in 1874 Waller recorded their memories, which became the narrative chapters of the Last Journals.
Friends and correspondents (letter from Bambarre, February 1871); Waller then edited the journal into print.
The Banian men whose violence fills the Nyangwe diary had been hired at the coast through Kirk.
Stanley recruited the Nasik men, Wainwright among them, and sent them up to Livingstone in 1872. Stanley also gave Livingstone the boy Majwara.

threads_out.note: Livingstone died still believing the Lualaba at Nyangwe was the Nile. Stanley's 1874–77 expedition, launched partly to finish his work, circled Lake Victoria and then followed the Lualaba down from Nyangwe with Tippu Tip's escort, proving it was the Congo.

Before he was a reporter, Stanley, then living in Arkansas, joined the Confederate army, was captured at Shiloh in April 1862, enlisted in the Union army to get out of a Chicago prison camp, and later deserted from the Union Navy.
